beats.text: This is Maya's first YouTube video. She spent two whole weekends making it.
She hit upload, refreshed the page, and waited.
Three views. And one of them was her mom.
If that sounds familiar, this video is for you.
Over the next eight minutes, we'll follow Maya through her first year on YouTube, and fix every mistake she makes, one at a time.
By the end, you'll know what actually makes a channel grow.
First, Maya needs to understand how YouTube decides what to show.
YouTube doesn't push videos out. It pulls them toward people.
Every time someone opens the app, it has millions of videos to choose from, and only a few spots on the screen.
So it tries to guess which video this one person will actually enjoy.
To guess well, it watches what viewers do.
Do they click? How long do they stay? Do they come back for more?
YouTube even asks some viewers directly, with quick surveys about whether they liked what they just watched.
So the algorithm isn't a gatekeeper you have to trick. It follows the audience.
Make something people click, watch, and enjoy, and YouTube will show it to more people like them.
That's the whole game. Everything else in this video is how to play it.
Maya's first mistake: her channel is about everything.
A baking video. A travel vlog. A video game review.
Each one reaches a different crowd, so nobody has a reason to subscribe.
So she asks herself three questions.
What could I make a hundred videos about?
Who, exactly, is this for?
And why would they pick me over anyone else?
Her answer: quick, cheap dinners for busy students.
It's specific enough that the right person instantly thinks: that's for me.
Later, she can widen it. But starting narrow makes her far easier to find, and far easier to remember.
A clear niche tells both viewers and YouTube who your videos are for.
Next: the click.
Maya's video is called, my cooking video number four. The thumbnail is a blurry frame of a frying pan.
On a busy home page, it's invisible.
Your title and thumbnail are a promise. In a split second, they answer one question: what do I get if I click?
So Maya rewrites the promise.
New title: five dinners for under ten dollars.
New thumbnail: one finished plate, her face reacting, and three big words.
Good thumbnails are simple. One subject, strong contrast, and text you can read on a phone.
Maya checks hers at the size of a phone screen. If she can't tell what it is in one glance, it goes back to the drawing board.
Good titles spark curiosity, but they never lie. If the video doesn't deliver, people leave, and YouTube notices.
Maya makes two versions, and tests them against each other.
In this example, the new one gets clicked almost twice as often.
Same video. Better promise.
Now people are clicking. But a lot of them leave in the first few seconds.
Her old intro: a spinning logo, some music, and, hey guys, welcome back to my channel.
Thirty seconds before anything happens.
So she opens with the payoff instead.
A sizzling plate on screen, and one line: this dinner costs three dollars, and takes ten minutes.
That's a hook. Show the result, confirm the promise from the thumbnail, and give people a reason to stay.
Cut the long intro. Cut the logo. Get to the good part, fast.
A good test: if a stranger skipped your first ten seconds, would they miss anything? If not, cut it.
On her retention graph, the steep drop at the start gets much smaller.
Next problem: the middle of her videos sags.
The retention graph in YouTube Studio shows exactly where people leave.
Every dip is a moment someone got bored.
So Maya edits tighter. She cuts the pauses, and the repeated steps.
She changes something on screen every few seconds: a new angle, a close-up, a line of text.
She plants small questions, like, stay to the end for the secret sauce. And then she actually pays it off.
She tells people where the video is going, and keeps moving forward.
And she ends the video the moment it's done, pointing straight to another video, instead of saying goodbye for a whole minute.
After every upload, she finds the biggest dip, and fixes that kind of moment next time.
When people watch longer, it's a sign they're enjoying it. And that's what YouTube wants to recommend.
Maya used to upload whenever she felt like it. Twice one week, then nothing for two months.
Now she picks a schedule she can actually keep: one video, every week.
A schedule matters less to the algorithm than people think. But it matters a lot to you.
Every video is practice. Video ten is better than video one. Video fifty is better than video ten.
She batches her work. She films two videos on Sunday, and edits during the week.
That rhythm means one bad week never breaks the chain.
And she stops chasing perfect. Done and uploaded beats perfect and stuck in a folder.
Then she adds Shorts.
Quick vertical videos that get shown to people who have never heard of her.
She cuts the best moment from each long video into a Short: the sizzle, the reveal, the price.
Shorts bring in new eyes. Long videos turn them into fans.
Some of the people who find her through a Short tap through to her channel, and stay for the longer videos.
She also turns her best idea into a series: dinner for under five dollars, week after week.
And she links her videos together with end screens and playlists, so one view leads to the next.
Every Sunday, Maya spends fifteen minutes in YouTube Studio.
She checks three things.
Click-through rate. Are people clicking when they see her thumbnail?
Average view duration. Are they staying?
And returning viewers. Are they coming back?
Low clicks? Work on the title and thumbnail.
Early drop off? Work on the hook.
Few returning viewers? Work on the series.
Over time, she spots patterns: which topics get clicked, which ones keep people watching, and which ones bring in subscribers.
She doesn't compare herself to giant channels. She only tries to beat her own last video.
Finally, she treats her viewers like people, not numbers.
She replies to comments in the first hour after a video goes live.
She pins the best questions, and turns them into her next videos.
She posts polls, and asks what they want to cook next.
She even features a viewer's recipe in one video, and that viewer shares it with all of their friends.
Viewers who feel heard come back. And people who come back are what turn a channel into a community.
One year later.
Maya has made fifty two videos. Most did okay. A few did great. And one took off.
Not because of a trick. Because each video was a little better than the last.
Her click-through rate went up. Her viewers stayed longer. And more of them came back, every single week.
So here's the whole thing, in one line.
Make videos for one clear viewer. Earn the click. Keep the promise. And get a little better every time.
Now go make your next video. And press upload.
